title: Adani Group Denies Airline Plans After Reuters Reports Aviation Ambitions
excerpt: Adani Enterprises called reports 'entirely baseless' in an exchange filing, a day after Reuters cited two sources saying the conglomerate was weighing a new carrier to challenge IndiGo and Air India's duopoly.
body:
• Adani Enterprises denied reports it was considering launching an airline, calling them "entirely baseless" in a stock exchange filing on Friday.
  • Reuters had reported, citing two sources with direct knowledge, that the group was weighing a new carrier — or acquiring a stake in an existing one — to challenge IndiGo and Air India's combined 90% market share.
  • The Adani Group has separately approached the government to relax a rule barring operators of Mumbai and Delhi airports from holding more than 10% stake in a scheduled airline.
  • India's aviation market remains heavily concentrated, with IndiGo commanding 65% and Air India 25%, raising policy concerns about over-dependence on two carriers.

Adani Enterprises on Friday flatly denied reports that the Adani Group was evaluating plans to enter the airline business, calling media coverage of the move "entirely baseless and factually incorrect" in an exchange filing.

The denial came a day after Reuters, citing two sources with direct knowledge, reported that billionaire Gautam Adani's conglomerate was considering launching a new airline or acquiring a stake in an existing carrier — a move that could reshape competition in a market dominated by IndiGo and Air India.

Shares of Adani Enterprises fell more than 3% on Thursday after the Reuters report. IndiGo dropped over 1%, while SpiceJet surged 10% on speculation it could be an acquisition target.

What Reuters Reported

According to Reuters' sources, the Indian government had privately encouraged large business groups, including Adani, to consider starting an airline. The nudge followed heightened scrutiny of Air India after its fatal Ahmedabad Dreamliner crash last year, and IndiGo's operational crisis in December when it cancelled thousands of flights due to a pilot shortage, stranding passengers and triggering government intervention to cap surging airfares.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=xtu8Yaoh5Oc

"It's a difficult business, but Adani wants to consider it in the national interest."

— Source with direct knowledge, speaking to Reuters

The sources said no final decision had been made and that all options were on the table, including buying a stake in an existing airline. Internal discussions were described as being in initial stages with no timeline.

Adani is Asia's second-richest person with a net worth of around $89 billion. His ports-to-cement conglomerate operates eight airports in India, including two in Mumbai, and has an $11 billion aviation infrastructure expansion strategy.

The Regulatory Hurdle

Separately, the Economic Times reported on Thursday that the Adani Group has approached the government seeking to dilute a clause in concession agreements that bars operators of Delhi and Mumbai airports from holding more than a 10% stake in a scheduled airline, according to Reuters.

https://x.com/CNBCTV18News/status/2080538468942483602

The restriction, part of public-private partnership agreements signed when major airports were privatised roughly two decades ago, applies to both Adani Group (which holds a 74% stake in Mumbai airport) and GMR Group (which operates Delhi airport). Any amendment would require the solicitor general's opinion and cabinet approval.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation is examining the proposal, according to Bloomberg. Sources within the ministry told the Economic Times that the aviation landscape has changed since the original agreements were drafted.

"There is no formal proposal before the government. These are preliminary discussions at best."

— Civil aviation ministry sources, per Economic Times

Rival airlines are expected to oppose any rule change over concerns about conflicts of interest in airport slot allocation, particularly at congested hubs like Mumbai.

India's Aviation Duopoly Problem

The backdrop to the discussion is India's extreme market concentration. IndiGo commands a 65.4% domestic market share, while Air India — which has absorbed Vistara and AirAsia India — holds about 25%. Together, they control roughly 90% of domestic capacity.

That concentration has created policy concerns. When IndiGo's pilot shortage triggered mass cancellations in December, the disruption cascaded across India's entire aviation ecosystem. Loss-making Air India, meanwhile, has faced a string of audit lapses amid intense scrutiny since the Ahmedabad crash that killed 260 people. SpiceJet, the next largest carrier, is battling financial challenges and salary delays.

India is one of the world's fastest-growing aviation markets, with plans to expand its airport network from 74 in 2014 to 350–400 by 2047. But the history is littered with failures: Kingfisher, Jet Airways, Go First, Air Deccan, and Air Costa have all collapsed over the past 15 years, done in by high taxes, fierce competition, and supply-chain challenges.

The Embraer Connection

Analysts have linked Adani's aviation interest to its proposed manufacturing partnership with Brazilian aerospace firm Embraer. An airline could serve as a launch customer for locally produced aircraft, creating a vertically integrated aviation ecosystem spanning airports, ground handling, pilot training, maintenance, and manufacturing.

"Adani's foray has the potential to reshape India's aviation landscape," said Rajan Mehra, former India head of Qatar Airways. He added that India must also focus on robust regulatory safeguards and a level playing field for all airlines.

What's Next

The contradiction between Reuters' sourced reporting and Adani Enterprises' categorical denial leaves the situation unresolved. As recently as December, Adani's youngest son Jeet Adani told Reuters the group was not interested in airlines because of thin margins. "Our comfort and our core competency is in creating hard assets on the ground," he said at the time.

Whether the denial settles the matter or the regulatory push on stake limits signals longer-term intent, the episode has reignited debate about whether India's aviation market needs a well-capitalised third player — and whether Adani, with its airport empire and deep pockets, is the right one to build it.
